claim: Cell cortex remodeling during cell division is a result of myofilament-driven contractility of the cortical membrane-bound actin meshwork.

claim: Little is known about the interaction between individual myofilaments and membrane-bound actin filaments.

evidence_reasoning: This is a primary finding directly observed in the experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: Tension builds up between the ends of myofilaments, resulting in compressive stress exerted to single actin filaments, causing their buckling and breakage.

claim: The mechanism of filament fragmentation and compaction may contribute to actin turnover and cortex reorganization during cytokinesis.
source_text: This mechanism of filament fragmentation and compaction may contribute to actin turnover and cortex reorganization during cytokinesis.

claim: The actin cortex consists of a thin actin meshwork bound to the inner cytosolic face of the plasma membrane by various anchor proteins.

claim: A minimal actin cortex (MAC) was developed consisting of actin filaments coupled to a supported lipid bilayer via biotin neutravidin bonds.
source_text: To mimic the cell cortex, we developed a 'minimal actin cortex' (MAC) consisting of actin filaments coupled to a supported lipid bilayer via biotin neutravidin bonds
evidence_reasoning: This describes the experimental system designed and constructed by the authors.

claim: The density of the actin layer in the MAC can be controlled by varying the amount of biotinylated lipids present in the lipid bilayer.
source_text: By varying the amount of biotinylated lipids present in the lipid bilayer, we have control over the density of the actin layer

source_text: Rabbit muscle myosin II was purified and reassembled forming bipolar synthetic myofilaments with a typical length of 500–600 nm

claim: MACs with various actin densities showed dynamic rearrangement of actin filaments and formation of actomyosin foci in an ATP-dependent manner after addition of myofilaments.
source_text: Time lapse imaging of MACs with various actin densities using total internal reflection fluorescence microscopy (TIRFM) showed a dynamic rearrangement of the actin filaments, and subsequently the formation of actomyosin foci in an ATP-dependent manner immediately after addition of myofilaments
evidence_reasoning: This is a direct experimental observation from TIRFM imaging.

claim: Actin pattern formation occurred at ATP concentrations between 0.1–1 µM in systems where ATP is enzymatically regenerated in 94% of the experiments.
source_text: Actin pattern formation occurred at ATP concentrations between 0.1–1 µM in systems where ATP is enzymatically regenerated (Table 1) in 94% of the experiments (n = 45 experiments).

source_text: At higher and lower ATP concentrations, actin pattern formation in the MAC is absent.

claim: Actin structure formation after ATP depletion has been reported for experiments using actin and myofilaments in solution.
source_text: Actin structure formation after ATP depletion has been also reported for experiments using actin and myofilaments in solution (Smith et al., 2007).

claim: At low ATP concentrations, myofilaments were predicted to function as active temporary crosslinkers, which may drive self-assembly of actin filaments into actin clusters.
source_text: At low ATP concentrations, myofilaments were predicted to function as active temporary crosslinkers, which may drive self-assembly of actin filaments into actin clusters.

source_text: Strikingly, myofilament addition to low density MACs displayed breakage events and compaction of actin filaments, resulting in their shortening over time in all experiments (n = 21

claim: An increase in fluorescence intensity along the remaining actin filament is often observed after a fragmentation event.
source_text: Furthermore, an increase in fluorescence intensity along the remaining actin filament is often observed after a fragmentation event
evidence_reasoning: This is a direct observation from fluorescence microscopy experiments.

claim: The fluorescence intensity proximal to the breakage site is approximately twice as high compared to the rest of the actin filament.
source_text: The fluorescence intensity proximal to the breakage site is approximately twice as high compared to the rest of the actin filament

claim: The fragment is dragged along the remaining actin filament by the myofilaments leading to its compaction.
source_text: suggesting that the fragment is dragged along the remaining actin filament by the myofilaments leading to its compaction
evidence_reasoning: This is an interpretation of the fluorescence intensity increase based on the experimental observations.

claim: Fragmentation and compaction contribute to the observed coalescence of actin fragments into single foci during the dynamic rearrangement of the actin filaments.
source_text: We propose that fragmentation and compaction contribute to the observed coalescence of actin fragments into single foci during the dynamic rearrangement of the actin filaments
evidence_reasoning: This is a mechanistic interpretation connecting multiple experimental observations.

claim: Upon binding of single myofilaments to individual actin filaments, directed movement of myofilaments along actin filaments and actin fragmentation at low ATP concentrations was observed.
source_text: Upon binding of single myofilaments to individual actin filaments, we observed directed movement of myofilaments along actin filaments and actin fragmentation at low ATP concentrations
evidence_reasoning: This is a direct observation from single molecule experiments.

claim: At high ATP concentrations, processive movement of myofilaments was barely visible, and fragmentation of actin filaments was absent.
source_text: In contrast, at high ATP concentrations, processive movement of myofilaments was barely visible, and fragmentation of actin filaments was absent
evidence_reasoning: This is an experimental observation comparing behavior at different ATP concentrations.

claim: Shortly after binding of myofilaments, actin filaments deformed and eventually broke, indicating that the force generated by a single myofilament is sufficient to break an actin filament.
source_text: Shortly after binding of myofilaments, actin filaments deformed and eventually broke, indicating that the force generated by a single myofilament is sufficient to break an actin filament
evidence_reasoning: This combines direct observation with an inference about force generation.

claim: The detected increase in the fluorescence intensity of actin filaments implies that actin fragments are further dragged along the remaining actin filaments by the myofilaments during their movement.
source_text: The detected increase in the fluorescence intensity of actin filaments implies that actin fragments are further dragged along the remaining actin filaments by the myofilaments during their movement
evidence_reasoning: This is an interpretation of fluorescence data to infer mechanical behavior.

claim: The velocity of myofilaments fluctuates during their movement along the actin filament.
source_text: The velocity fluctuates during the movement of the myofilament along the actin filament
evidence_reasoning: This is a quantitative observation from tracking analysis.

claim: Acceleration events are closely followed by an increase in the actin fluorescence, indicating that a breakage event occurred.
source_text: whereby acceleration events (Figure 3C, red arrowheads) are closely followed by an increase in the actin fluorescence, indicating that a breakage event occurred
evidence_reasoning: This correlates two measured parameters to infer a causal relationship.

claim: Phases of increasing tension between the ends of the myofilament lead to deformation of the actin filament and coincide with a decrease in velocity.
source_text: We hypothesize that phases of increasing tension between the ends of the myofilament lead to deformation of the actin filament and coincide with a decrease in velocity
evidence_reasoning: This is a hypothesis proposed to explain the observed velocity fluctuations.

claim: Phases of tension release immediately after actin filament breakage may result in acceleration of the myofilament.
source_text: while the phases of tension release immediately after actin filament breakage may result in acceleration of the myofilament
evidence_reasoning: This is a hypothesis to explain the observed acceleration events.

claim: The myosin filament aligns parallel to the actin filament and interacts with it via the myosin heads.
source_text: The myosin filament aligns parallel to the actin filament and interacts with it via the myosin heads
evidence_reasoning: This is based on established knowledge about myosin-actin interactions, supported by citation.

claim: One end of the myofilament (the 'leading end') is oriented towards the actin plus end (barbed end) and can walk along the actin filament while hydrolyzing ATP.
source_text: One end of the myofilament, which we will refer to as the 'leading end', is oriented towards the actin plus end (barbed end), as the filaments in a muscle, and can therefore walk along the actin filament while hydrolyzing ATP
evidence_reasoning: This is based on known myosin behavior and applied to the experimental system.

claim: The other end of the myofilament (the 'trailing end') is separated from the leading end by the approximately 160 nm long bare zone without myosin heads.
source_text: The other end of the myofilament, which we will refer to as the 'trailing end', separated from the leading end by the approximately 160 nm long bare zone (Al-Khayat et al., 2010) without myosin heads
evidence_reasoning: This structural information is cited from Al-Khayat et al., 2010.

claim: The trailing end's opposite orientation results in a much slower directed motion towards the actin plus end.
source_text: While the trailing end still interacts with the actin filament, its opposite orientation results in a much slower directed motion towards the actin plus end (Spudich et al., 1985; Sellers and Kachar, 1990).
evidence_reasoning: This is based on prior experimental work cited from Spudich et al., 1985 and Sellers and Kachar, 1990.

claim: Every myosin head independently follows the biochemical cycle consisting of ATP hydrolysis, binding to actin, powerstroke accompanied by phosphate dissociation, ADP dissociation, ATP binding, and finally detachment from actin.
source_text: Every myosin head independently follows the biochemical cycle consisting of ATP hydrolysis, binding to actin, powerstroke accompanied by phosphate dissociation, ADP dissociation, ATP binding, and finally detachment from actin
evidence_reasoning: This describes the well-established myosin biochemical cycle, cited from Howard, 2001.

claim: The heads on the trailing end either do not perform steps that would lead to a processive motion (probability of making a step pst=0), or make steps with a small probability (pst=0.1).
source_text: We assume that the heads on the trailing end still interact with the actin filament and go through the same cycle, but either do not perform steps that would lead to a processive motion (probability of making a step pst=0), or make steps with a small probability (pst=0.1).
evidence_reasoning: This is an assumption made for the modeling based on observed behavior.

claim: When a myosin head makes a step (step size d = 5 nm) it tries to move the whole myofilament towards the actin plus end, but other attached myosin heads are holding it back, thus generating friction.
source_text: When a myosin head makes a step (step size d = 5 nm (Howard, 2001)) it tries to move the whole myofilament towards the actin plus end, but other attached myosin heads are holding it back, thus generating friction
evidence_reasoning: This is a mechanistic interpretation combining known step size with inferred mechanical behavior.

claim: The myofilament trailing end functions mainly as a source of friction (an effective 'brake'), but is also moved towards the plus end by the pulling force exerted by the leading end.
source_text: The myofilament trailing end functions mainly as a source of friction (an effective 'brake'), but is also moved towards the plus end by the pulling force exerted by the leading end
evidence_reasoning: This is a mechanistic interpretation of the model's behavior.

claim: Since mainly the leading end is actively moving and the trailing end is either passively pulled or contributes only weakly to its own motion, tension builds up within the myofilament, and is transferred onto the actin filament as a compressive force.
source_text: Since mainly the leading end is actively moving and the trailing end is either passively pulled (pst=0) or contributes only weakly to its own motion (pst=0.1), tension builds up within the myofilament, and is transferred onto the actin filament as a compressive force.
evidence_reasoning: This is a mechanistic explanation derived from the model assumptions.

claim: If sufficiently high, this compressive force can cause buckling, and finally breakage, of the actin filament.
source_text: If sufficiently high, this compressive force can cause buckling, and finally breakage, of the actin filament
evidence_reasoning: This is a prediction from the mechanical model.

claim: After the breakage, the leading end can move unhindered further towards the plus end, while dragging along the broken-off part of the actin filament attached to the trailing end.
source_text: After the breakage, the leading end can move unhindered further towards the plus end, while dragging along the broken-off part of the actin filament attached to the trailing end
evidence_reasoning: This is a predicted consequence of the breakage event in the model.

claim: The trailing end can also attach again to the actin and further breakage events on the same filament can follow.
source_text: The trailing end can also attach again to the actin and further breakage events on the same filament can follow.
evidence_reasoning: This is a predicted possibility from the model dynamics.

claim: Actin filaments are modeled as flexible rods with bending rigidity EI = 60 nN μm².
source_text: In order to estimate the force needed to break an actin filament, we model the filaments as flexible rods with bending rigidity EI = 60 nN μm
evidence_reasoning: This uses established physical parameters for actin from literature.

claim: The force needed to buckle and break the filament is F = π² EI/l², which gives a force of 23 pN with the length l of the myofilament bare zone of 160 nm.
source_text: The force needed to buckle and break the filament is F = π2 EI/l2. With the length l of the myofilament bare zone of 160 nm, this gives a force of 23 pN.
evidence_reasoning: This is calculated using established mechanical theory applied to the experimental parameters.

claim: Actin filaments break when the radius of curvature of a bent filament decreases below 0.18 μm corresponding to the curvature 1/r = 5.6 μm⁻¹.
source_text: Actin filaments break when the radius of curvature of a bent filament decreases below 0.18 μm (Arai et al., 1999) corresponding to the curvature 1/r = 5.6 μm−1.
evidence_reasoning: This is cited from Arai et al., 1999.

claim: For 30 myosin heads, the force of 23 pN necessary to bend the filament could be reached at ATP concentrations of approximately 3 µM or lower.
source_text: For 30 myosin heads, the force of 23 pN, neccessary to bend the filament, could be reached at ATP concentrations of approximately 3 µM or lower
evidence_reasoning: This is a result from computational simulations.

claim: In the ATP concentration range used in the experiments (<100 µM), the average velocity of myofilament increased approximately linearly with ATP concentration.
source_text: In the ATP concentration range used in the experiments here (<100 µM, see also Table 1) the average velocity of myofilament increased approximately linearly with ATP concentration
evidence_reasoning: This is a result from simulations that matches experimental conditions.

claim: The average fraction of myosin heads attached to actin increased with decreasing ATP concentration.
source_text: The average fraction of myosin heads attached to actin increased with decreasing ATP concentration
evidence_reasoning: This is a result from simulations based on the biochemical cycle model.

claim: At low ATP concentration, the generated force was sufficiently high to continuously bend the actin filament, steadily increasing the curvature above the breakage threshold.
source_text: At low ATP concentration, the generated force was sufficiently high to continuously bend the actin filament, steadily increasing the curvature above the breakage threshold
evidence_reasoning: This is a result from simulations showing the conditions for breakage.

claim: At intermediate ATP concentrations, the force fluctuating near the threshold caused fluctuations in curvature, at times exceeding the curvature threshold and then relaxing again to a straight filament configuration.
source_text: At intermediate ATP concentrations, the force fluctuating near the threshold caused fluctuations in curvature, at times exceeding the curvature threshold and then relaxing again to a straight filament configuration
evidence_reasoning: This is a result from simulations describing dynamic behavior.

claim: At even higher ATP concentrations, the threshold force was reached for too short periods for sufficiently high curvature to develop.
source_text: At even higher ATP concentrations, the threshold force was reached for too short periods for sufficiently high curvature to develop
evidence_reasoning: This is a result from simulations explaining why breakage doesn't occur at high ATP.

claim: To bend and break the actin filament, the myofilament has to be attached to the actin for sufficient time, and sufficient force has to be generated, requiring a certain mean number of heads being attached to actin at any given time.
source_text: To bend and break the actin filament, the myofilament has to be attached to the actin for sufficient time, and sufficient force has to be generated, requiring a certain mean number of heads being attached to actin at any given time.
evidence_reasoning: This is a mechanistic conclusion from the modeling and experimental results.

claim: Given the small number of interacting myosin heads, a large fraction of heads must be in the bound state to generate sufficient force.
source_text: Given the small number of interacting myosin heads this translates to a requirement that a large fraction of heads is in the bound state.
evidence_reasoning: This is a logical conclusion from the force requirements and head number.

claim: In the assay, the requirement for a large fraction of bound heads was achieved with low ATP concentrations.
source_text: In our assay this was achieved with low ATP concentrations.
evidence_reasoning: This explains how the experimental conditions met the theoretical requirements.

claim: It is tempting to speculate that actin breakage by myofilaments in vivo is governed by the ATP level in the cell.
source_text: It is tempting to speculate that actin breakage by myofilaments in vivo is governed by the ATP level in the cell.
evidence_reasoning: This is explicitly stated as speculation about in vivo relevance.

claim: Recent evidence exists that ATP levels indeed vary significantly inside living cells.
source_text: Recent evidence exists that ATP levels indeed vary significantly inside living cells (Imamura et al., 2009).
evidence_reasoning: This cites evidence from Imamura et al., 2009.

claim: Physiological ATP concentrations, derived from methods that provide averaged ATP levels with no high spatial and temporal resolution from cell extracts, are usually found in the millimolar range.
source_text: However, physiological ATP concentrations, derived from methods that provide averaged ATP levels with no high spatial and temporal resolution from cell extracts, are usually found in the millimolar range (Beis and Newsholme, 1975).
evidence_reasoning: This cites established knowledge about ATP concentrations from Beis and Newsholme, 1975.

claim: Skeletal muscle myosin II (used in this study) has a lower duty ratio and is therefore less processive than non-muscle myosin in cells.
source_text: Here it is important to mention that skeletal muscle myosin II (used in this study) has a lower duty ratio and is therefore less processive than non-muscle myosin in cells (Harris and Warshaw, 1993; Wang et al., 2003).
evidence_reasoning: This is established knowledge cited from Harris and Warshaw, 1993 and Wang et al., 2003.

claim: By lowering the ATP concentration in the assay, the duty ratio of myofilaments was increased and thereby made them more processive, similar to non-muscle myosin.
source_text: By lowering the ATP concentration in our assay, we increased the duty ratio of our myofilaments and thereby made them more processive (supplementary text in 'Material and methods', Figure 5, Movie 5), similar to non-muscle myosin

claim: The observation that lowering ATP increases processivity is in line with previous studies.
source_text: which is in line with previous studies (Humphrey et al., 2002; Smith et al., 2007; Soares e Silva et al., 2011).
evidence_reasoning: This cites supporting evidence from multiple prior studies.

claim: Processivity of myofilaments in animal cells may be controlled by phosphorylation of myosin light chains through other proteins that modify the kinetic rates of the biochemical cycle and thereby increase the duty ratio of the myosins.
source_text: Moreover, processivity of myofilaments in animal cells may be also controlled by phosphorylation of myosin light chains through other proteins that modify the kinetic rates of the biochemical cycle and thereby increase the duty ratio of the myosins shifting the observed behavior to a region of high physiological ATP concentrations (Tan et al., 1992; DeBiasio et al., 1996; Matsumura et al., 2001).

claim: Myofilaments fragment and compact membrane-bound actin in the in vitro system.
source_text: In conclusion, our findings show the distinct functions that myosin motors can execute. In our minimal system, myofilaments fragment and compact membrane-bound actin.

claim: Single myofilaments can interact with actin in such a way that sufficient force can be generated to break the filament, without either the myofilament or the actin being firmly attached to a solid support or scaffold.
source_text: We directly show that single myofilaments can interact with actin in such a way that sufficient force can be generated to break the filament, without either the myofilament or the actin being firmly attached to a solid support or scaffold.

claim: Fragmentation and compaction by myofilaments contributes to the observed large-scale pattern formation of actomyosin networks in other in vitro systems.

source_text: We propose that the observed fragmentation and compaction of membrane-bound actin filaments by myosins in our in vitro system may serve as a possible general mechanism for actin turnover and actin cell cortex remodeling.

claim: Directed movement accompanied by actin filament fragmentation only occurred at low ATP concentrations between 0.1–1 µM.
source_text: In our minimal system directed movement accompanied by actin filament fragmentation only occurred at low ATP concentrations between 0.1–1 µM
evidence_reasoning: This is a specific experimental observation about ATP concentration dependence.

claim: Lower ATP concentrations are expected to increase the duration of the actin-bound post-working stroke state of the myosin head, thus increasing the duty ratio and processivity.
source_text: The lower ATP concentrations are expected to increase the duration of the actin-bound post-working stroke state of the myosin head, thus increasing the duty ratio and processivity (Howard, 2001).

claim: Extremely low ATP concentrations are not sufficient for myosin motor activity.
source_text: Extremely low ATP concentrations are on the other hand not sufficient for myosin motor activity.

claim: Low ATP trajectories are on average longer than high ATP trajectories indicating a higher processivity at low ATP conditions.
source_text: Comparison of the trajectories illustrates that low ATP trajectories are on average longer than high ATP trajectories indicating a higher processivity at low ATP conditions

claim: The number of tracked myofilaments at low ATP concentration with a dwell time greater than 900 ms was more than six times higher than at high ATP concentration.

evidence_reasoning: This is a quantitative result from tracking experiments.

claim: High ATP concentrations lead to a faster detachment of myofilaments from actin filaments than at low ATP concentrations.
source_text: High ATP concentrations therefore lead to a faster detachment of myofilaments from actin filaments than at low ATP concentrations
evidence_reasoning: This is an interpretation of the dwell time and trajectory data.

claim: The increase in processivity due to ATP deprivation is necessary for the processive movement and a prerequisite for fragmentation and compaction of actin filaments.
source_text: We propose that the increase in processivity due to ATP deprivation is necessary for the processive movement and a prerequisite for fragmentation and compaction of actin filaments.

claim: Each active myosin head goes through a biochemical cycle consisting of six head states.
source_text: In the model of the myofilament interaction with actin, we assume that each active myosin head goes through the following biochemical cycle consisting of six head states
evidence_reasoning: This is based on established knowledge of myosin biochemistry used in the model.

claim: The myosin step size is d = 5 nm.
source_text: The myosin step size is d = 5 nm (Howard, 2001).
evidence_reasoning: This is a known parameter cited from Howard, 2001.

claim: The myosin heads of the leading myofilament end always perform a step as a result of the powerstroke between the states 3 and 4.
source_text: The myosin heads of the leading myofilament end always perform a step as a result of the powerstroke between the states 3 and 4.

claim: The trailing myofilament end moves along actin with approximately ten-times slower speed than the leading end.
source_text: This value is based on the observations that the trailing myofilament end moves along actin with approximately ten-times slower speed than the leading end (Sellers and Kachar, 1990).

claim: Every myosin head attached to the actin filament is described as a spring with a spring constant equal to the myosin head stiffness κ = 1 pN nm⁻¹.
source_text: Every myosin head attached to the actin filament is described as a spring with a spring constant equal to the myosin head stiffness κ = 1 pN nm−1 (Kaya and Higuchi, 2010).

claim: After every step and after every detachment of a myosin head the forces are equilibrated by moving the myofilament along the actin filament.
source_text: After every step and after every detachment of a myosin head the forces are equilibrated by moving the myofilament along the actin filament.

claim: The result is a net movement of the whole myofilament towards the actin plus end, with fluctuating tension force, velocity and number of attached myosin heads.
source_text: The result is a net movement of the whole myofilament towards the actin plus end, with flucuating tension force, velocity and number of attached myosin heads, the mean values of which depend on the ATP concentration.

claim: The median length of the myofilaments determined with AFM was 560 nm.
source_text: The median length of the myofilaments determined with AFM was 560 nm

claim: The length of the bare zone without myosin heads in the central part of the myofilament is 160 nm.

claim: Both ends of the myofilament are 200 nm long.

evidence_reasoning: This is calculated from the total length minus the bare zone length.

claim: There are on average 110 head pairs on each myofilament.
source_text: With four myosin head pairs around the myofilament circumference per every 14.5 nm (Woodhead et al., 2005), there are on average 110 head pairs on each myofilament.
evidence_reasoning: This is calculated using structural information from Woodhead et al., 2005.

claim: The average number of interacting heads is 30 per myofilament.
source_text: Assuming further that only those heads oriented towards one side, that is, one quarter, can interact with the actin filament, and that only one head of the head pair is favorably oriented to interact, we estimate the average number of interacting heads as 30 per myofilament.
evidence_reasoning: This is calculated based on geometric and structural considerations.

claim: The persistence length of actin is lp = EI/(kT) = 15 μm.
